Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, with system performance measured by similarity metrics like BLEU, BERTScore, or MTEwer against multiple human references. Consequently, the quality of these references fundamentally limits both the performance of learned systems and the validity of their evaluation. This project investigates the impact of data quality on evaluation by comparing three distinct image description datasets: a high-quality dataset created for the VTBC video captioning challenge, two professional datasets derived from comments by image hosts, and a large-scale crowdsourced dataset from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The analysis reveals that the professional datasets contain numerous grammatical errors and factual mistakes, whereas the VTBC descriptions are almost error-free. When evaluating state-of-the-art models like BLINK and MVHDT, their predicted descriptions often exhibit significant errors when assessed against the noisy professional data, yet remain undetected when measured against the VTBC dataset. These findings suggest that similarity-based metrics can yield misleading results if reference data are flawed, potentially masking deficiencies in both models and evaluations. To address this, we propose integrating an error annotation dataset into the evaluation process, offering a more reliable method for assessing automatic image description systems in the presence of imperfect references. This approach could also guide future efforts to improve systems using such data. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/linguee/ReferenceQuality.

Consequently, we derive an exact formula for the ratio of single to tripartite complexity and provide precise expressions for the single : bipartite : tripartite complexities. Finally, we outline how this methodology can be extended to compute higher-order complexities. Ultimately, the Euler-Arnold flow serves as a powerful tool for analyzing complexity, offering insights applicable to various mathematical and physical domains. These efforts require theoretical frameworks capable of describing a broader range of systems and initial conditions, ideally through first principles. We specifically examine the limitations of current hydrodynamic models when applied to small systems and highlight the potential of lattice hydrodynamics to address these challenges. Additionally, we review recent hydrodynamic findings from heavy ion collisions and summarize current progress and future directions in hydrodynamics within small quantum systems.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over an observation span of approximately a decade has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental challenge in assessing this claim is determining the typical interval between X-ray transients for neutron stars. This paper examines the likelihood of an individual neutron star being observed in a steady, non-outbursting state within the X-ray sensitivity limits of current telescopes. It derives a general formula for the duration a star spends in a quiescent state detectable by a specific instrument between two outbursts, and calculates the expected number of such detections based on a specific outburst recurrence time and a total monitoring duration. Applying this approach to nine neutron stars in the Galactic Centre for which at least two outbursts have been recorded, we derived lower limits for their outburst recurrence times. These results indicate that, with current telescope sensitivity and a one-decade monitoring period, it is improbable to find an additional source like XPer-9 between two outbursts if its recurrence time is under $\sim$100 years. Consequently, explaining the nine known stars requires a median outburst interval exceeding $\sim$100 years, which aligns with the difficulty of detecting such long intervals with current facilities. Given these findings, attributing all X-ray variable sources in the Galactic Centre to neutron stars with intervals longer than $\sim$100 years is unlikely, as it would also make it improbable to detect any further examples with existing or planned observatories. Furthermore, we critique the assumption that an outburst must conclude and the system return to a previous steady state before a new one can begin. Finally, we speculate on the possible origins of the long intervals between outbursts observed in certain neutron star systems.

As a direct result, we derive an effective fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for finding a minimum size edge set to convert a bipartite graph into a split-bipartite graph. Finally, we establish that this problem is also solvable in polynomial time when the graph's diameter is restricted as an additional parameter. Potential applications of these results are discussed in this work and by Amir and Gutner [1]. Performance degradation techniques serve as a vital complement to side-channel attacks, enabling the extraction of cryptographic secrets at speeds unachievable by attacks alone. This synergy has been pivotal in uncovering cache and branch misprediction leaks. However, a limiting factor in this synergy is the efficacy of the degradation method itself; overly aggressive strategies introduce significant noise, undermining extraction success. While prior research has primarily focused on performance tracing to identify optimal points for such techniques, these methods are incompatible with high-performance, stealthy side channels. Furthermore, existing approaches fail to ensure that workload execution times remain constant, a critical requirement for cache attacks which rely on precise timing. In response to these gaps, we introduce a novel performance degradation method that guarantees constant execution times. Despite this assurance, the method is so effective at slowing down workloads that we integrate a real-time CPU frequency scaler to mitigate the associated execution time overhead. Implementing this technique, we couple it with a flush+prime attack to demonstrate its compatibility with high-side-channel workloads. Our results show a tenfold improvement over the previous state-of-the-art performance degradation method. Utilizing this new approach as a counterpart to a recent cache side channel, we reveal that an end-to-end extraction pipeline can operate nearly twice as fast as feasible with any prior combination of side channel and degradation methods. As a final demonstration of its potency, we adapted this method to counteract FlushOut, a recent attack targeting remote systems executing Crafted PDFs. Our adaptation successfully bypassed OutByte's best strategies for counteracting trace-based side channels, extracting keys from workloads that earlier methods could not handle. To facilitate adoption by the academic community, we open-sourced the method as an open-library function compatible with various side-channel workloads and attacks. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/Anubhav-1999/HyperDegrade.

Coordination represents a fundamental capability for systems of intelligent agents, whether human or robotic, operating in shared environments. This study examines how a team of strategic workers performs three distinct tasks using a network of limited capacity, while also exploring the potential for expanding that network. We find that when tasks generate positive spillovers, agents are motivated to select the most demanding task over the most capable network. Conversely, if spillovers are negative, agents avoid the most difficult task and instead utilize the most capable network. These outcomes align with the predictions of the Harberger-Mas-Colell model of fiscal federalism, which posits that agents cluster in jurisdictions with stricter regulations when spillovers are positive, but disperse when they are negative. This principle holds true regardless of whether spillovers are driven by congestion or by the scarcity of network capacity. Additionally, we observe that increasing a network's capacity does not necessarily lead to higher throughput, particularly when tasks exhibit strategic complements. These conclusions remain valid whether agents possess complete information or rely on a symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium with incomplete information. The proposed model offers insights into workforce distribution across regions of varying regulatory strictness, as well as decisions regarding infrastructure investment and expansion. Furthermore, it applies to scenarios involving the allocation of air traffic among airports of different sizes and the distribution of data traffic across internet links of varying capacities. Simulation results demonstrate that these findings also extend to environments where tasks are best described by utility functions rather than linear forms. This study investigates the global atmospheric circulation regimes of Earth using a spectral model with triad truncation at $T_{L}=30$ km, which is approximately twice as high as the configuration used by Selub and Ward (2021). The model employs a simplified baroclinic initial state with a uniform radiative equilibrium profile. Consistent with prior research, the system exhibits a transition from super-rotational equatorial zonal flows to a combination of barotropic and baroclinic eddy turbulence as the differential rotation $\beta$ increases. However, the specific transition points for these circulation shifts are sensitive to the initial zonal wind profile, vertical heat distribution, and angular momentum conservation at the lateral boundaries. Furthermore, the eddy heat flux successfully counteracts the radiative stability of the initial baroclinic state, facilitating the development of baroclinic eddies. When the triad truncation is lowered to $T_{L}=20$, a similar transition from cyclostrophic to geostrophic turbulence occurs as $\beta$ increases, though the resulting circulation state differs from that observed at $T_{L}=30$. At $T_{L}=20$ and $\beta=1$, the system displays a distinct pattern of alternating zonal jets, a feature not seen at the higher truncation level. These findings indicate that the simulated global circulation regime depends on a combination of planetary parameters, including rotation rate, atmospheric heat distribution, and triangular truncation, mirroring the variation of circulation patterns with planetary vorticity and heat driving forces on real planets. Additionally, the results suggest that on actual planets, increasing Coriolis force (via lower planetary vorticity) shifts the circulation regime from cyclostrophic to geostrophic turbulence, while enhancing thermal driving (up to a saturation point) promotes the formation of eddies and zonal jets within that regime. These conclusions hold true for both planetary atmospheres with significant initial meridional temperature gradients, such as gas giants, and those without, like terrestrial planets. Finally, the study considers the impact of friction and discusses the validity of the assumed lateral boundary condition.

We present a real integral representation for the reciprocal Gamma function, derived through the convolution of two recently introduced regularized sums of gamma functions. This formulation incorporates a complex regularization parameter and converges for real parts greater than zero. Leveraging this real integral representation, we achieve a regularized real integral representation for a product involving this rec regularization parameter and a Gaussian integer power term. Finally, utilizing this latter representation alongside the standard complex power definition, we construct a complex integral representation that explicitly highlights the real part of the rec regularization parameter within the exponent. These integral representations are employed to establish several identities among various complex power definitions, as well as between the Gamma function and its Bessel counterpart. These findings are anticipated to benefit numerical computations of the Gamma function and its Bessel variant, and may also prove useful in theoretical investigations, for instance, in quantum field theory. Hydrodynamic theories provide effective descriptions of complex systems by simplifying the underlying microscopic dynamics. In this study, we develop a rigorous hydrodynamic framework for Bose gases using a recently introduced stochastic formulation of quantum kinetics in classical phase space. This approach establishes exact stochastic quantum hydrodynamic equations, derived from a noise-driven generalization of the Boltzmann-Langevin equation that incorporates both binary and non-binary binary collisions. By performing a gradient expansion, we derive a deterministic version of these equations that extends the range of validity for the binary collision approximation. Furthermore, we incorporate quantum effects through a further expansion, creating a classical-like hydrodynamic model suitable for highly excited systems. To illustrate the application of this framework, we derive a generalized Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer hydrodynamic model that accounts for quantum, binary collision, and non-linear effects. The underlying stochastic quantum kinetic and hydrodynamic theories offer comprehensive descriptions of out-of-equilibrium open quantum systems, integrating quantum, statistical, thermal, and dissipative phenomena. Potential applications span the study of quantum phenomena in classical hydrodynamic models, the analysis of experimental data from ultracold gases and heavy-ion collisions, and the creation of improved quantum initial conditions for hydrodynamic models used in such contexts. Additionally, this stochastic kinetic theory could serve as a theoretical foundation for classical molecular dynamics-based methods, similar to how Born-Majorana and Weizsacker-Willer approximations underpin semi-classical Wigner-based approaches. This framework represents a significant contribution to quantum statistical mechanics, with relevance to ultracold gases, heavy-ion physics, molecular dynamics, and mathematics.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at handling large-scale data across various domains, their deployment on resource-constrained devices like smartphones and IoT systems remains challenging due to high computational costs and memory requirements. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a promising technique to transfer knowledge from complex models to simpler architectures, achieving performance in tasks such as classification, recognition, and generation. Recently, architectures where a student model learns from one or more teacher models have gained significant traction. These structures typically consist of a complex model acting as the "ground" teacher and a simpler one serving as the "learning" teacher, with the student optimizing to match the outputs of both. This dual-source approach often yields superior results compared to traditional methods that utilize only a single teacher. The rise of such configurations has spurred interest in specialized networks designed specifically for knowledge distillation, including high-level, student-specific architectures. Furthermore, there is growing focus on the "learning" teacher itself, leading to frameworks where a simple model is distilled by a complex teacher and a simple student, potentially delivering better outcomes than conventional approaches. This survey examines these evolving architectures, alongside related concepts like co-training, multi-task learning, and consistency regularization. It also addresses practical implementation challenges, such as optimizing the complexity of intermediate architectures and balancing gradients among multiple teachers. Finally, the survey discusses recent regularization strategies, contrasts different architecture-based methods, and explores hybrid approaches combining architecture-based and regularization-based techniques. Additionally, it covers student-specific frameworks, surveys existing work, and highlights recent progress in auto-regressive methods for constructing these specialized networks.

Significance testing, specifically the paired-permutation test, has been underutilized in deep learning due to the high computational cost of exact methods and the unavailability of suitable approximations for certain structures. This work introduces an efficient algorithm for the exact paired-permutation test, applicable to nine previously unsupported test statistics. Evaluations using both synthetic data and state-of-the-art image generation and completion models demonstrate that our method offers an significant performance improvement over the best existing alternatives, achieving a 14x to 200x gain in efficiency for certain combinations of data size and test statistic type. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is openly available as a new statistic-based function within the recently released PyRho package (https://github.com/haofanwang/PyRho).

Using the AMPT multiphase transport model, we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Our results show that, unlike the elliptic flow $v_2$, the triangular flow $v_3$ exhibits minimal dependence on centrality. Once the influence of initial geometry is accounted for, the ratio $v_3/\epsilon_3$ rises with increasing transverse particle density, mirroring the behavior of $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Furthermore, the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ observed experimentally is primarily driven by the change in participation line symmetry from triangular to rectangular as transverse momentum moves from 1 to 4 GeV/$c$. Finally, the $v_3$ values predicted by AMPT align better with measured data than those derived from hydrodynamic models initialized via a causal molecular dynamics framework, indicating that AMPT generates a more significant initial spatial anisotropy. These findings suggest that initial-state models may overestimate the "rigidity" of matter created in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the variation of $v_3$ with multiplicity offers a valuable constraint for both initial-state and evolution models. This work was performed by the PHENIX Collaboration.

Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where a single goal represents a significant positive outcome, whereas failure to score or conceding a goal yields negative returns that are difficult to avoid. These dynamics create a non-linear environment particularly challenging for policy gradient methods, which often struggle to generalize in the face of substantial reward shifts. Conversely, value-based approaches find it difficult to distinguish between actions that result in similar rewards, such as scoring versus preventing an opponent from scoring. To address these limitations, we introduce a two-stage training framework that combines distributional and policy gradient methods to determine optimal behaviors during high-strisk moments. This work also examines the suitability of state-of-the-art soccer tracking data for this specific task. Our numerical findings indicate that this hybrid method outperforms both distributional and gradient baseline algorithms in simulated environments. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates superior results compared to standard baselines when evaluated on real-world soccer data.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $E_{\rm cm}-M_X$ spectra, employing a robust method to confirm the rest frame isotropy of candidates. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $p_{\rm tot}=2.5\,\text{ab}^{-1}$, we search for the decay chain $B^0\to K^0s A$, followed by $K^0s\to\pi^+\pi^-$ and $A\to\ell^+\ell^-$ ($\ell=e,\mu$), analyzing sidebands in the $K^0s$ mass distribution to establish lower limits on the visibility of two-body decays. Consequently, we derive bounds on the branching ratio for $B^0\to K^0s A$ and outline strategies for investigating the particle's properties. Our findings indicate that for decay lengths exceeding $c\tau\sim 1\,\text{m}$, no viable limit can be set at Belle II using the $B^0\to K^0s A\to K^0s\ell^+\ell^-$ channel; however, we propose an alternative search based on one-body decays into visible plus missing energy final states. Furthermore, we report lower limits on the branching ratio for $B^0\to K^0s\ell^+\ell^-$ and establish limits on related processes. These results yield constraints on the seesaw scale for Dirac-like neutrinoless Majoron emission, as well as on the coupling between the $Z$ boson and dark sector particles. At a future 100 GeV Higgs factory, we anticipate that new physics goals can be effectively met at this class of collider. Such experiments would enable precise measurements of the decay width, determination of the mixing angle with neutral mesons, and exploration of the nature of the lightest supersymmetric particle. These objectives represent ideal science goals for a 10 GeV collider operating at a muon collider, a proton synchrotron, or a fixed-target facility. We conclude by outlining the search strategy at a muon collider

This paper offers a qualitative examination of potential applications and limitations of using contextualized embeddings to identify diachronic semantic change. We begin by detailing our manual verification process for confirming diachronic semantic change and for identifying contextualized embeddings that warrant further investigation. Our findings indicate that pre-trained language models are increasingly effective at detecting known instances of diachronic semantic change, as evidenced by the clustering of historical embeddings corresponding to changed meanings along specific axes. However, our analysis also uncovered numerous examples where these models cluster together changes in register, grammatical shifts, or even unrelated meanings. We provide illustrative cases of these phenomena and discuss possible causes. Ultimately, we conclude that while contextualized embeddings are a valuable starting point for automating the detection of diachronic semantic change, additional methods are necessary to distinguish between genuine semantic shifts and other linguistic variations. The detailed account of our manual verification protocol is available at https://github.com/linguisticted/linguisticted_reviews. Our work sits at the intersection of historical linguistics and NLP; specifically, we focus on diachronic changes, which involve linguistic evolution over time, contrasting with synchronic changes that represent simultaneous variations such as dialectal differences or register variations (e.g., formal versus informal language). Common instances of diachronic change include grammatical shifts (e.g., gender agreement), lexical alterations (e.g., words acquiring new meanings), and stylistic evolution (e.g., slang entering mainstream vocabulary). Although significant progress has been made in automating these changes through distributional models and contextualized embeddings, there has been less effort in analyzing the errors these approaches make. Our study fills this gap, and we anticipate that the detailed errors identified here will inspire future research into distinguishing between various types of linguistic variation. Furthermore, our findings have implications for NLP tasks that assume word embeddings capture fixed semantic representations, such as word ranking systems for suggesting alternatives or translations. These applications would benefit from incorporating a method to detect and filtering out words undergoing semantic, grammatical, or registral change, as their fixed vector-space models may no longer be reliable. Regarding our methodology, our framework for identifying interesting embeddings for potential diachronic change builds upon the approach by Conneau et al. (2012), which compared embeddings from a single source (WikiText 10). We first generate embeddings from multiple historical versions of a text source using a range of pre-trained contextualized models. We then calculate the Mahalanobis distance between each word's historical embeddings and its representation from the latest text

This study addresses the bias present in the line-of-sight (LoS) component of vector magnetic field maps generated by neural network (NN) inversion codes. Unlike other components of the LoS, this bias exhibits a symmetric "butterfly" pattern centered at zero, distinguishing it from typical inversion biases that favor positive or negative values. We demonstrate that this symmetry arises because the NN learns a non-linear mapping between the true LoS component and its absolute value |LoS|. Consequently, this behavior represents a form of information loss during the reconstruction process, as the network cannot distinguish between positive and negative inputs when they yield identical outputs. To mitigate this issue, we developed a post-processing method that reduces the bias without introducing additional errors into already unbiased components (Bx and By). Employing a dataset of synthetic "ground truth" images, we trained an NN to correct the biased LoS component using the full data as input. When applied to the "ground truth," this correction algorithm successfully recovered the original values with high precision. We subsequently tested this approach on real observational data from the Vector Solar Optical Concentric Ellipse (VSOCE) instrument, a novel solar helioseismology instrument under development. The results indicate that the bias-mitigation method effectively reduces the symmetry of the remaining butterfly pattern. Furthermore, when comparing the corrected VSOCE data against NN-reconstructed Vector Of Field COne (VOC) data from the HMI instrument on the same observations, the corrected VSOCE data aligns more closely with the "true" LoS values of the VOC data than the uncorrected version does. Finally, we applied the correction to vector magnetic field data from the VSOCE and the HDC instrument on a plasma flux rope observed by the JWO/Telescope 1 (formerly GST/1), which was the target of recent multi-wavelength observations by the ST/RX (formerly XRT), NRC/Imager A (formerly IA), and NRC/Imager B (formerly IRA) instruments. It remains uncertain if bulge expansion drives the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. We found that while central concentrations vary with B-band magnitude across the entire dataset, the bulge-dominated galaxies are significantly larger and more rotationally supported than the pure disk galaxies for equivalent central luminosities. Using stellar mass ($M_*$) and gas plus stellar mass SFR density ($\eta$) as coordinates, we fitted a two-component function to the local MS: $log(M_*) = A_0 + B_0 \times log(\eta) + C_0 \exp(-D_0 \times log(\eta))$. Extending this to redshift $z \le 1.5$, we distinguished the linear and turnover segments by fitting separate one-component functions. The sample was then divided into bulge-dominated and non-bulge-dominated galaxies based on the best-fitting central concentration parameter. We discovered that bulge-dominated galaxies at $z \sim 1.5$ exhibit higher specific SFRs than the overall median for a given $M_*$, whereas at $z \sim 0$, the specific SFRs of these galaxies are lower than the median. Consequently, the fraction of bulge-dominated galaxies must increase from $z \sim 0.5$ to $z \sim 1.5$ for $M_* > 10^{10.4} M_{\odot}$, but show little variation below this mass limit. Finally, we applied different weights to the non-bulge and bulge components of the MS at each redshift to test whether the evolution of this fraction accounts for the MS flattening at high masses. Our results indicate that while bulge growth correlates with flattening, other physical processes are likely responsible for causing the MS to flatten at $log(M_*) > 10.4 - 10.5$. We present new constraints on the mechanisms responsible for accelerating the rotation of giant planets during their evolution. Golay complementary matrices (GCM) have recently attracted significant attention due to their potential applications in omnidirectional precoding for multiuser OFDM systems. By leveraging the newly proposed GCM constructions of negative order and existing GCA constructions of multiple dimensions, we derive several novel GCA constructions. Specifically, we establish construction methods for GCMs of order one from pairs of first-order GCMs with distinct negative orders, and for GCMs of order two from two first-order GCMs or two second-order GCMs. These derivations yield new GCA construction methods of three dimensions from two GCA sets of three dimensions with different orders. Furthermore, we introduce a technique to convert a GCA of three dimensions into another of three dimensions with a reduced cross-correlation level, and subsequently generalize this approach to convert an $N$-dimensional GCA into a "higher-order" $N$-dimensional GCA with lower cross-correlation. Key contributions include a unified framework for contrasting unsupervised and supervised extraction methods, a novel contrastive learning approach, and a two-step optimization strategy; additionally, the method's superiority over existing techniques is validated through experiments on nine datasets. The proposed framework offers a viable solution for classification tasks involving high-dimensional datasets, potentially finding applications in domains such as chemistry, biology, and medicine. This research is classified under Feature Extraction and Contrastive Learning, with the dataset contribution noted as No. Our framework consists of three primary stages: (I) determining a low-dimensional target space, (II) an unsupervised phase to establish a mapping from high- to low-dimensions without labels, and (III) a supervised phase where a high-dimensional feature vector is contrastively learned from low-dimensional vectors using contrastive loss, ultimately yielding an optimized low-dimensional representation.

Although large language models (LLMs) achieve high performance across numerous natural language processing tasks, integrating structured knowledge remains a potent method for enhancing specific applications, such as medical domains. This paper introduces a framework that boosts LLM performance in medical applications by incorporating knowledge graphs (KGs). Our approach employs a dual mechanism: a retrieval-based method to generate semantically enriched text and a knowledge-based technique to directly guide generation. Evaluations show that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art language and knowledge-based methods in medical question answering, summarization, and dialogue generation. Additionally, our system demonstrates improved results on specialized tasks like medical multiple-choice questions and medical entity recognition. We open-sourced our framework at https://github.com/Pranav-1777/SKILL. Our study reveals that retrieval-based techniques excel at filling missing information, whereas knowledge-based methods are more effective at correcting hallucinations. Furthermore, incorporating a clinical decision support system into our knowledge graph further improves performance on medical multiple-choice questions and medical mentions classification. Ultimately, our framework achieves a win rate of 58.6% on multiple-choice questions using only a BERT-base backbone, surpassing the current state-of-the-art open-weight model, T5-3B. These findings indicate that our framework has the potential to scale effectively to larger models.

Non-linear interactions between electromagnetic fields and vacuum are a significant area of research with potential practical applications. In this study, we investigate the non-linear Madelung charge within a static, spherically symmetric Ansatze framework. Using the waveform of a black hole shadow as an observable, we determine the anatomic structure of black holes. The results indicate that the shadow radius initially contracts and then expands as the Madelung parameter increases. Furthermore, we analyzed the thermodynamic behavior across an anatomic cross-section. It was found that, similar to Penrose energy and irreducible area, the temperature exhibits non-monotonic behavior along this cross-section. These findings suggest that the non-linear Madelung charge influences both the shadow radius and thermodynamic properties. Consequently, these characteristics can serve as a useful tool for exploring the anatomic structure and thermodynamics of black holes in the context of modified gravity theories. This work extends the application of shadow observables, which were previously utilized to examine the impact of extra dimensions, spin, and magnetized charge on black hole temperature and entropy. The study concludes by outlining the significance of this research. Reconstructing quantum states in continuous variables is essential for both fundamental research and practical applications. While numerous methods exist, their effectiveness varies depending on the specific scenario. This study introduces a straightforward technique to reconstruct the Wigner function from time-bin tomograms, enabling the examination of non-classical features and the detection of classical-like behavior within certain scenarios. We demonstrate that switching from a negative to a positive Ward identity in the Wigner function provides a reliable indicator of non-classicality in the entanglement between remote quantum systems. Furthermore, we reveal that this entanglement exhibits a sudden change during a transition from quantum to synchronized behavior between subsystems. Additionally, we show that the entanglement between any pair of subsystems within a composite system can be represented as a curve on a "bird's-eye view" plot of the corresponding Wigner function in the W-basis. This visualization offers a clear depiction of non-classicality and its variations, complementing the analysis performed in the Q-basis. Similarly, the evolution of entanglement among different pairs of subsystems in the composite system can be clearly observed on the bird's-eye view in the W-basis, alongside a manifestation of this evolution in the Q-basis. These findings suggest that the W-basis provides an effective framework for detecting and analyzing quantum-to-classical transitions, as well as the emergence of non-locality and other characteristics, in both individual systems and their subsystems. We conclude this work by outlining the potential applications of these results. The referenced techniques are accessible via the IQPSTM software, available at https://github.com/IQPSTM. This study demonstrates that certain well-known biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, described by a specific collection of geometric operators, are not recurrent, as defined by a particular class of recurrent operators. Furthermore, we establish that all lightlike Biharmonic hypersurfaces are recurrent when using these specific recurrent operators. Additionally, we prove that Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ ($n\geq 1$) contains no hypersurface with mean curvature vector given by a specific form that is both biharmonic and recurrent under these operators. Finally, we show that circular cylinders $M^{n}(r_1,r_2)=S^{n-1}(r_1)\times S^{1}(r_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ ($n\geq 2$) with distinct radii ($r_1\neq r_2$) are biharmonic, but are recurrent if and only if a particular condition involving the radii is met. Several other examples are also examined.

For any rational number $p/q$, the regular expressions over $\mathbb{Q}_{p/q}$-recognisable sets were defined by Salomaa in 1973, utilizing terms from $p$-adic analysis. We establish that a subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathcal{R}(\pfrac{p}{q})$-regular if and only if it is 1-n recognisable for some coprime integer $n$ and the ratio $(pqn)/q$ is a rational integer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for $|q| > 1$, there exists a context-free language that is $\mathcal{R}(\pfrac{p}{q})$-recognisable but is not a context-free language over the alphabet of $q$-adic integers. These findings imply that for $|q| > 1$, the hierarchy of $r$-recognisable set families for $r \in \mathbb{N}$ is strict when considered from the perspective of context-free languages. Additionally, we show that a language is eradicatable (meaning no context grammar requires it to be derived infinitely often) if and only if it is both a context-free language and $\mathcal{R}(\pfrac{p}{q})$-recognisable. As a corollary, we provide a decidable method to determine whether a given context-free language is eradictable. Finally, we present a decidable test to verify if a finite state automaton over $\mathbb{Z}$, defined by regular expressions over $\pfrac{p}{q}$, adheres to a specific context-free grammar. This work extends the applications of automatic structures and recognizes sets within the domain of formal language theory and theoretical computer science. We anticipate that these results will find utility in number theory, particularly in the study of $p$-adic analysis.

This study investigates the acoustic emission (AE) generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant speed and a varying pulling angle. By applying a fractal analysis to the AE spectrum, a fractal dimension of 1.5 was identified across different pulling angles and pulling speeds. Furthermore, when normalized by the Euclidean dimension, the fractal dimension of the acoustic emission intensity remained constant as the pulling angle varied. A similar invariance was observed when the pulling speed changed. These findings support a model in which multiple micro-fractures occur simultaneously during the tape's fracture process. Additionally, the fractal dimension of the total acoustic emission intensity showed no correlation with the fractal dimension of the AE spectrum itself. The coexistence of two fractal dimensions within the same spectrum implies that the slope of the acoustic emission spectrum's fractal region is determined solely by the fractal dimension of the total intensity. Ultimately, the fractal analysis of the acoustic emission confirms that the micro-fractures responsible for the AE exhibit a self-similar distribution of sizes. This self-similarity validates the application of earthquake-like models, which have been utilized to describe the fractal nature of cracks in other systems. Such self-similar, multi-scale micro-fractures likely give rise to the "crackling noise" heard during various fracturing processes. Supporting this conclusion, the Weibull distribution of inter-event times between acoustic emissions aligns with the power-law distribution of their amplitudes, a relationship characteristic of self-organized criticality systems. These phenomena suggest that the "earthquake-like" dynamics of frictional sliding also govern the opening and closing of micro-fractures as the pulling speed or angle changes. Despite these similarities to seismic events, the fractal dimension of the acoustic emissions in this system is higher than that typically associated with earthquakes, indicating that the underlying micro-fractures are more self-similar than those found in geological earthquakes. This increased self-similarity may be attributable to the smoother, more homogeneous surface of the laboratory adhesive tape compared to the heterogeneous, rough surface of tectonic plates. The fractal dimension of the acoustic emission during this peeling process is comparable to that observed in other materials, such as granite, when fractured under uniaxial compression. Consequently, the fractal dimension serves as a useful metric for characterizing the self-similarity of micro-fractures across different materials. Neural network-based scores derived from deep learning classifiers have achieved substantial success in security and safety-critical domains. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these approaches for point cloud models remains underutilized. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing technique tailored for point cloud models. We empirically demonstrate that integrating transformation-specific noise with our method substantially enhances the accuracy of smoothing-based bounds compared to traditional baselines. Furthermore, we apply TPC to elevate the reliability of certification for point cloud models in real-world scenarios, yielding significant improvements in the tightness of certified bounds across various noise models and point cloud transformations. Our findings also reveal that TPC can strengthen the quality of bounds for point cloud models subjected to deeper and more complex transformations, such as the recently proposed adaptive transformation. Finally, we establish the first certification results for 3D point clouds under realistic LiDAR sensor noise, confirming the feasibility of this goal through the application of TPC. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/UselessHou/TPC-Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

The integration of geometry into theoretical computer science has recently gained traction, yielding significant outcomes in areas such as program semantics, static analysis, and synthesis. In contrast, its application to program testing remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces a geometric framework for automated testing, offering a unified model that encompasses both symbolic execution and random testing. Leveraging this framework, we developed the Getae tool to equip C/C++ programs with a "meta-tester" capable of systematically verifying other tests against the program's execution. Empirical results from this study demonstrate that the optimized symbolic execution aligns with industry standards, while the overall framework delivers performance gains compared to traditional testing methods. By enabling the systematic evaluation of tests—a capability currently absent in the field—this geometry-based approach is likely to yield further benefits. Additionally, the framework can be extended to other compilers and testing environments to facilitate the systematic assessment of compiled code and automated test suites. Regarding the underlying mathematical foundation, we utilized a recent geometry-based theory for the Hoare logic of C/C++ developed by our group; alternatively, this work could be adapted to rely on other geometric theories of Hoare logic for languages supporting C-like dynamic memory allocation, such as those by Amadio et al. or Ouaknine et al. Finally, the proposed framework is amenable to further development for specialized testing goals, including the systematic construction of regression tests to address specific errors and the verification of properties related to test coverage.

This paper provides an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory and avoiding p-adic Hodge theory. The approach relies on characterizing the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions via Kummer theory applied to the underlying Galois representation. An appendix by B. Senni offers an explicit description of this characterization using logarithmic differentials. While the main text utilizes a specific formulation of adelic points on the p-adic upper half-plane, the results extend to any other suitable model. Additionally, the article includes an explicit version of the local lifting lemma at prime 2, which is required for certain applications. These explicit constructions are anticipated to be valuable in various contexts, including the construction of eigenforms and their associated modular parametrizations. Furthermore, the explicit nature of these results is expected to support computational efforts in identifying new Serre newforms and parametrizing their congruence ideals via ideal class groups. A significant outcome of this work is Corollary 9.1, which establishes that the contributing ideals are precisely those admitting an Atkin-Lehner eigencharacter, a finding that aligns with the results reported in reference [20]. Finally, this explicit construction may assist in addressing a question posed by Xiao-Wu Chen regarding the existence of Hilbert modular forms in the context of explicit computations involving Hermitian modular forms and their congruences.

Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an intrinsic capability to detect global damage through changes in electrical conductivity and utilize shape-sensitive reconstruction techniques, like electrical impedance tomography (EIT), to estimate image-based damage locations with high precision. However, existing methods lack the ability to determine damage size accurately or distinguish between multiple defects. This research introduces a novel approach combining a genetic algorithm (GA) with EIT to precisely identify crack dimensions and multiple cracks within uniaxially damaged nanocomposites. The method's effectiveness and the practical utility of the GA-EIT technique were validated using a laboratory-scale three-point bend setup with a pre-existing artificial crack. Furthermore, the strategy was applied to a carbon nanofiller-reinforced electroactive glass fiber/uniaxially oriented electroactive nanocomposite (GF/UCN) structure, successfully identifying and sizing a known defect and distinguishing between two separate cracks in a U-shaped specimen. These findings demonstrate that the GA-EIT framework offers a powerful solution for precisely characterizing damage size and multiple defects in structurally safe nanocomposites, contributing to the development of intelligent self-sensing structures. Consequently, this could eliminate the need for embedded self-healing mechanisms, as precise damage identification alone would be sufficient to enable autonomous self-healing capabilities. We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that incorporates specific geometric vectors and operators, offering a unified perspective on various coordinate systems. This approach enables the definition of vector bases aligned with curvilinear coordinates, facilitating their straightforward manipulation. Additionally, we define directional operators along arbitrary vectors, allowing for their easy handling without requiring a priori selection of a specific basis. We demonstrate the application of this framework to Euclidean spaces utilizing curvilinear, generalized spherical, and a recently introduced anisotropic spherical coordinate system. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between this framework and the theory of Finsler manifolds.

We demonstrate that if a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ admits a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree $T$ that is not a line, then $\Gamma$ must contain a separating subgraph $\Lambda$ for which $A(\Lambda)$ stabilizes an edge in $T$. Consequently, all minimal actions of $A(\Gamma)$ on trees are classified as disjoint amalgamated products and Guirardaud moves. Furthermore, we explicitly construct a family of right-angled Artin groups admitting two distinct decompositions into disjoint Guirardaud-move related amalgamated products of $A(\Gamma)$ along subgroups that are not conjugate. These constructions reveal that the decomposition into minimal actions on a tree, as established by JSJ theory for right-angled Artin groups, is not necessarily unique. Finally, we apply these findings to identify obstructions for certain groups from the literature acting on trees. Specifically, we provide a novel proof that the commutator of a braid group $B_n$ ($n\geq 3$) generates a normal subgroup with a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree, and we show that the outer automorphism group of a direct product of two non-abelian free groups also admits such an action. Additionally, we correct an error in the proof of Theorem 1.5 found in the work of Meier and Rolfsen titled "An invariant for right-angled groups acting on trees" (arXiv:1801.06014). The corrections involve the section detailing the $\Phi$-JSJ decomposition and its uniqueness, as well as the final paragraph of Section 3.1. These adjustments also necessitate minor modifications to the proofs of Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3.

This study extends the Chebyshev-Mu and Newton-Mu techniques, originally designed for dense matrices, to sparse matrices for accelerated convergence. Unlike BHO and GK, which require a preconditioner matrix identical in sparsity to the target, our approach only needs the initial matrix, offering greater flexibility. We term this method the "N-Mu" technique. Comparative tests against BHO, GK, and Newton show that for a 3D elastic wavefield modeling matrix with 0.3 sparsity, the 3rd-order 1-Nu and 2-Nu methods are 2.75× and 4.2× faster per iteration than Newton, respectively, while the 3-Nu method is 7× faster; against BHO and GK, all higher-order methods demonstrate significant speedups. For a matrix with 0.5 sparsity, the 2nd-order 1-Nu and 2-Nu methods outperform Newton by 1.75× and 2.25×, and the 3-Nu method by 4.5×. These results confirm that higher-order methods achieve notable gains for 0.3–0.5 sparsity levels. Furthermore, for matrices with sparsity exceeding 0.5, the N-Mu method surpasses iterative methods (BHO, GK, 1-Nu) by 2–3× and the direct method (CHOL) by 1.5×. Contextual linear bandits represent a significant area of research with widespread practical applications. In this study, we investigate a learning protocol for a point-to-point setting where the agent and environment are separated, and the input vector remains hidden from the agent. We introduce two novel protocols: a learning approach where the remote agent requires no prior knowledge of the contextual linear bandit problem, and an optimization method where the local agent is fully aware of the problem details. Prior to each round, the environment sends a one-dimensional projection of the current context to the local agent, who then selects an action based on the full context. Consequently, the information available to the agent at each step is strictly less than that in a standard contextual linear bandit scenario. Therefore, minimizing expected regret is challenging due to the missing context in the observed context-linear bandit problem. We establish an upper bound on the expected regret for both deterministic and stochastic environments. Furthermore, we define a lower bound for the stochastic environment that matches the upper bound in the stochastic case, confirming its optimality. Our theoretical findings indicate that the missing context does not necessarily hinder the minimization of expected regret if an appropriate protocol is adopted. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism capable of generating supersonic turbulence in optically thin, outer protoplanetary disks. However, this instability relies on a source of vertical buoyancy stability, and its development can be hindered by the cooling rates necessary to activate it. Specifically, gas must cool below a critical rate, which in the outer regions of disks depends on the ratio of dust to gas mass. While the early oligarchic growth of planetestons typically accounts for dust enrichment in these areas, this assumption may not hold if significant turbulence persists from the disk's formation due to other hydrodynamical instabilities. In such scenarios, the dust-to-gas ratio could exceed enrichment levels required for VSI onset. To investigate this possibility, we incorporated an evolving dust component into global simulations of VSI in the outer disk regions. Our results indicate that an initial dust-to-gas ratio of approximately 0.005 is necessary to trigger the instability. Consequently, if other instabilities like the gravito-turbulence are present at the outer edges during collapse, the VSI may be suppressed by a high dust-to-gas ratio resulting from that activity. This suppression could help explain why brown dwarfs and stars formed in clusters often exhibit low angular momenta and rotate as differential rotators with low tachocline shear, conditions unfavorable for the magnetorotational instability. Furthermore, the VSI's activation in outer regions offers a potential mechanism for enriching the dust-to-gas ratio in the inner regions through radial inflow, potentially facilitating the formation of super-Earths and planetary cores there. Ultimately, future observations of molecular emission lines from outer regions, combined with measurements of gas and dust vertical structures, are essential for verifying these conclusions. Additionally, the VSI may play a role in generating magnetic fields in these regions via the dynamo effect, although field strengths remain limited by the instability's origin layer, likely producing only weak fields of approximately $10$ G. This limitation could account for the absence of radio emission from brown dwarfs and low-mass stars, distinguishing them from classical asteroids and pulsars. Distinguishing the VSI-driven dynamo from $\alpha-\Omega$ dynamos in brown dwarfs and stars will be crucial for determining the magnetic field origins of emerging planets.

This study examines harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that possess constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. These findings are significant for analyzing the stability of gradient shrinking solitons under the Ricci flow. Additionally, we confirm that steady 2-soliton solutions in dimension three cannot exist. Regarding applications, we derive several rigidity results for 3-dimensional $\alpha$-Einstein solitons (where $\alpha$ is a positive constant) under various geometric conditions. Ultimately, we characterize 3-dimensional $\alpha$-Einstein solitons with constant scalar curvature as $\mathbb{Q}$-Gaussian shrinkers or $\mathbb{R}$-Gaussian shrinkers. Furthermore, we provide a complete classification of 3-dimensional gradient shrinking solitons that are Einsteinian or have the product of positive and negative curvatures remaining constant. Throughout this work, we utilize the Bochner technique as a primary methodological tool. The research areas covered include 35-12, 53-02, 53-03, and 58-01. This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a complex model from data distributed across heterogeneous sources, where some nodes possess sufficient information to train specific model components while others lack the necessary data. Traditional solutions relying on gradient descent-based federated learning methods often fail due to data scarcity at certain nodes. In contrast, our proposed Random Walk (RW) approach enables the model to learn effectively by leveraging data-only nodes as bridges; the model iterates through these nodes multiple times, gathering sufficient information for convergence. Our method requires no modification of underlying data or communication of raw data between nodes. We validate RW through simulations on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, we provide theoretical proof of convergence for a linear model with feature engineering and extend this analysis to a general non-convex setting. Simulation results confirm that RW outperforms existing methods across various data distributions and initial parameter conditions. Potential applications include scenarios where data privacy prevents centralized access, such as healthcare, and situations involving data silos where transferring data between sources is impractical.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of scientific inquiry, yet selecting an appropriate testing method for specific research questions remains challenging. This study demonstrates that workflow techniques can enhance the robustness of BF analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate how these same workflows facilitate the exploration of posterior distributions and the calculation of predictive probabilities, thereby supplying additional context for the BF values themselves. Our approach utilizes the R package RWBy (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RWBy), which enables the construction of such workflows through a user-friendly graphical interface. We present several examples across diverse research domains, including psychology, neuroscience, and genetics, to highlight the practical utility of this methodology. Ultimately, we argue that adopting a multiple-prior Bayesian hypothesis testing strategy via these workflows yields more comprehensive and informative statistical conclusions. Discourse markers, such as \textit{however}, indicate semantic or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent advances in natural language understanding have moved toward predicting the specific relation expressed by these markers through compositional semantic representations. These models typically rely on sentence pairs without explicit labels to learn the mapping between a marker's use and its meaning. Nevertheless, existing representations fail to capture the fact that discourse markers connect specific predicates or predicates to attributes, nor do they account for competing relations between identical markers and pairs of clauses or sentences. Applying this technique to the FORD corpus to create a formal resource, we demonstrate that a neural network trained on this resource can accurately predict the relation of over forty markers using almost no supervised data. When evaluated against two professional annotations of the SemEval task, this network performed comparably to prior systems that had been specifically trained on such data. We also assessed the resource and the related unsupervised learning approach against human judgments from a small, manually annotated subset of the Asrmc corpus. The resulting metrics indicate that both the resource and method achieve high accuracy. Additionally, we briefly outline how this resource and approach can be extended to a corpus of written comments to extract semantic and pragmatic information about slurs and hate speech. Invariant manifolds constitute a fundamental concept in the analysis of dynamical systems, playing a pivotal role in the study of local asymptotic stability and the construction of global phase portraits. This work offers a comprehensive overview of invariant manifolds, detailing their definition, characterization, and graphical depiction for both linear and nonlinear systems. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach to determine the type of invariant manifold associated with an equilibrium point within nonlinear systems. Leveraging this framework, we demonstrate that specific invariant manifolds described by fractional order linear systems do not exist when implemented in a fractional order context. Consequently, we establish the nonexistence of certain invariant manifolds in specific nonlinear fractional order systems along the line of reasoning used for linear systems. Finally, we propose a general methodology to verify the compatibility of invariant manifolds in any given fractional order system. The proposed techniques are applicable to all systems of differential equations involving Caputo, Riemann-Liouville, or other fractional derivatives, provided a suitable definition of invariance is adopted. As a byproduct of this research, we correct an error in the proof concerning the local asymptotic stability of a homoclinic orbit in a Chua circuit with a commutative fractional derivative. The discussed methods are of significant value for investigating the global dynamics of systems with integer and fractional orders. This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale arises from tree-level seesaw dynamics, while the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We identify and analyze a stable metastable vacuum region within the parameter space that aligns with current observational constraints. Focusing on the phenomenologically relevant region where the atmospheric neutrino mass is approximately $10^{-2}$ eV, we determine that the dark matter density of $10^{-2} < \Omega_{\rm DM} < 1$ requires a top quark pole mass between 132.6 and 132.7 GeV. At this specific mass scale, the electroweak Higgs vacuum sits precariously near the stability boundary, a phenomenon we attribute to the light neutrino mass generating a non-attractive correction to the Higgs potential. Conversely, for lighter dark matter densities ($\Omega_{\rm DM} < 10^{-2}$), the model calls for lower seesaw scales, which in turn necessitate weaker couplings to explain the target density; here, the correction from the sub-eV neutrino becomes negligible. Under these conditions, dark matter stability is ensured by the freeze-out mechanism, and the precision of the $\Omega_{\rm DM}$ prediction relies on the freeze-out density rather than the ultimate stability of the vacuum. To achieve $10^{-2} < \Omega_{\rm DM} < 1$ with atmospheric neutrino masses around $10^{-2}$ eV, the dark matter particle must have a mass near 50 GeV, while the other parameter clusters are: $\mu \sim 100$ GeV, $M_2 \sim 130$ GeV, $y_\nu \sim 10^{-5}$, and $\lambda_S \sim 0.1$. We confirm that all predictions conform to current experimental limits and propose several theoretically motivated dark sector extensions capable of broadening the range of achievable dark matter densities. Finally, we outline the characteristic signatures of this minimal model at hadron colliders and future colliders, as well as in precision measurements at low-energy facilities.
